segments.text: <curious> Everything so far needed n to be a positive integer. Now we ask the wild question: what could one plus x to the one half, or to the minus three, possibly expand to? This is a JEE extension, and it changes the rules.

The problem is obvious. For a positive integer power there's a clear last term to stop at. But there's no natural place to stop when the power is a half or a minus three — you can't choose r things out of half a thing. So either the idea breaks, or it continues forever.

Look at the coefficient written the long way. n C r is n, times n minus one, times n minus two, and so on for r factors, all over r factorial. This falling-factorial form is defined for any real n — nothing in it demands that n be a whole number.

And here's the single observation that unlocks everything. For a positive integer n, that product eventually includes the factor n minus n, which is zero, and every later coefficient dies — that's why the series stops at r equals n. But if n is minus three, or one half, the product never hits zero, so the series simply never stops.

Because it's now an infinite series, it only sums to the true value of one plus x to the n when the size of x is less than one. Outside that range the partial sums blow up and the expansion is meaningless. This convergence condition is not a technicality you can wave away.

Picture it on a number line. Between minus one and one, the series converges — that green band is the safe zone. At or beyond one in either direction, it diverges. So before you use the series, always arrange the binomial so the smaller quantity sits in the x slot and stays inside that band.

One firm rule to carry through this subtopic: there are no n C r symbols here, because n C r is undefined when n is negative or fractional. You use the falling-factorial coefficient instead. Anytime you catch yourself writing a combination symbol with a non-integer on top, stop — that's the wrong tool.
Here's the formula sheet for any index. Everything here lives under the condition that the size of x is less than one — hold that as a permanent footnote on every line.

The general binomial series: one plus x to the n equals one, plus n x, plus n times n minus one over two factorial, x squared, plus n times n minus one times n minus two over three factorial, x cubed, and on forever. It's the same shape as before, just with falling-factorial coefficients that never terminate.

The general term follows the same pattern: T r plus one is n times n minus one, down to n minus r plus one, over r factorial, times x to the r. Now r runs over all non-negative integers, with no upper limit.

Four special expansions are worth memorising outright. One minus x to the minus one is one plus x plus x squared and so on — the geometric series. One plus x to the minus one is the same with alternating signs, one minus x plus x squared minus.

One minus x to the minus two is one plus two x plus three x squared, its general term being r plus one times x to the r. And one plus x to the minus two is the same with alternating signs. These four show up constantly, so know them cold.

For a general negative integer power, one minus x to the minus p equals the sum of p plus r minus one choose r, times x to the r. This clean combination form is the right tool for negative-integer powers — no undefined symbols anywhere.

And the workhorse of the whole applications side: when the size of x is very small, everything beyond the linear term is negligible, so one plus x to the n is approximately one plus n x. That single line powers every estimation problem.

The cast: n is any rational index now, positive, negative, or fractional; r is unbounded because the series is infinite; and as always every quantity is a pure number. Keep the convergence condition attached and these formulas are safe to use.
Let's turn the series into three reliable techniques you'll actually use on problems.

First, why the series continues at all. The general term written in falling-factorial form is defined for any real n. The termination we saw for positive integers is just the special case where the factor n minus n kills everything past r equals n. Remove that accident and the series naturally runs forever.

Second technique: expanding a plus b to the n for a general power. You cannot apply the series directly unless the bracket leads with a one, so factor out the dominant term first. Pull a to the n outside, leaving one plus b over a inside.

Concretely, a plus b to the n equals a to the n, times one plus b over a, to the n — and you must choose a as the larger part so that the size of b over a is less than one, keeping you inside the convergence band. Then apply the series to the bracket and multiply the a to the n back in.

Third technique: identifying a numeric series as a binomial expansion. Match the first three terms to the template one, then n y, then n times n minus one over two factorial, y squared. That gives you two equations in the two unknowns n and y.

The slick step is to divide the third equation by the square of the second. All the scaling cancels, leaving n minus one over two n on one side. Solve that single ratio for n, then back out y — and the series sums to one plus y, to the n.

Fourth, approximation. For small x, truncate after the linear term: one plus n x. If the question demands more precision, keep the next term too, n times n minus one over two, x squared. Match the number of terms you keep to the accuracy asked.

And for the curious: the honest proof of the whole series uses Taylor's theorem, where the falling-factorial coefficient turns out to be one over r factorial, times the r-th derivative of one plus x to the n, evaluated at x equals zero. You don't need that for problems, but it's why the pattern is exactly what it is.
Example one is a foundation drill: write the first four terms of one plus x to the minus two, and state where it's valid.

Feed n equals minus two into the general series. The terms are one, plus minus two x, plus minus two times minus three over two factorial, x squared, plus minus two times minus three times minus four over three factorial, x cubed. Just be careful with the signs in each falling-factorial product.

Simplify each coefficient and the pattern is beautiful: one minus two x plus three x squared minus four x cubed, and so on, valid for the size of x less than one. Notice the coefficients are just the counting numbers with alternating signs — that's the signature of a minus-two power.
Example two is a JEE Main favourite: find the coefficient of x to the fourth in one minus two x, to the minus three.

For a negative integer power, switch to the clean combination form. One minus y to the minus p equals the sum of p plus r minus one choose r, times y to the r. Here p is three and y is two x. Don't try to force the falling-factorial by hand — use this.

The coefficient of y to the fourth is three plus four minus one choose four, which is six choose four, equal to fifteen. But watch — y is two x, so y to the fourth is two x to the fourth, which is sixteen x to the fourth. The two carries a factor of sixteen.
So the coefficient of x to the fourth is fifteen times sixteen, which is two hundred forty. The combination gave the fifteen; the substituted variable gave the sixteen; multiply them together.

Two traps live here. First, writing minus three choose four — that's undefined, because you can't put a negative on top of a combination. Second, forgetting the two to the fourth from y equals two x. Switch to the p plus r minus one form and keep the coefficient's power, and both traps vanish.
Example three is where the approximation earns its keep: estimate the fourth root of two hundred fifty five, without a calculator.

The move is to sit next to a perfect fourth power. Two hundred fifty five is two hundred fifty six minus one, which is two hundred fifty six times one minus one over two fifty six. And two hundred fifty six is four to the fourth — a clean fourth power we can pull out.

So the fourth root of two fifty five is four times one minus one over two fifty six, to the one quarter. Since one over two fifty six is tiny, apply one plus n x is about one plus n x, with n equal to a quarter. That gives four times one minus a quarter of one over two fifty six, which is four minus one over two fifty six, about three point nine nine six one. Remarkably accurate for one line of work.

Note what we did: we used only the first-order approximation, one plus n x. If the question wanted more decimal places, we'd keep the quadratic term as well. The precision you keep should match the precision you're asked for.

Example four is the Advanced showpiece: sum the infinite series one, plus three quarters, plus three times five over four times eight, and so on. There's no obvious pattern to add — so we identify it as a binomial series.

Match to the template. The second term gives n y equals three quarters. The third term gives n times n minus one over two factorial, y squared, equal to fifteen over thirty two. Now divide the third by the square of the second: all the scaling cancels and you're left with n minus one over two n equals five sixths.

<excited> Solve that ratio: six times n minus one equals ten n, giving n equals minus three halves. Then from n y equals three quarters, y is minus one half. So the series is one minus one half, to the minus three halves — which is one half to the minus three halves, equal to two to the three halves, which is two root two. A wild-looking sum collapses to a clean surd.

segments.text: <curious> Ab tak sab kuch ke liye $n$ ko positive integer hona zaroori tha. Ab hum jungli sawaal poochhte hain: $1+x$ power one-half, ya power minus three, aakhir expand ho sakta hai kya? Yeh JEE extension hai, aur yeh rules badal deta hai.

Problem saaf hai. Positive integer power ke liye ek clear last term hota hai rukne ke liye. Par jab power one-half ya minus three ho toh rukne ki koi natural jagah nahi — aap aadhi cheez mein se $r$ cheezein nahi chun sakte. Toh ya idea toot jaayega, ya hamesha chalta rahega.

Coefficient ko long way mein dekho. $n\,C\,r$ hai $n$, into $n-1$, into $n-2$, aise hi $r$ factors tak, poora $r$ factorial ke upar. Yeh falling-factorial form kisi bhi real $n$ ke liye defined hai — isme kuch bhi $n$ ke whole number hone ki maang nahi karta.

Aur yeh raha woh single observation jo sab kuch kholta hai. Positive integer $n$ ke liye, woh product aakhir mein factor $n-n$, jo zero hai, include kar leta hai, aur har baad ka coefficient mar jaata hai — isiliye series $r$ equals $n$ pe rukti hai. Par agar $n$ minus three, ya one-half ho, toh product kabhi zero nahi hota, toh series bas kabhi rukti hi nahi.

Kyunki ab yeh ek infinite series hai, yeh $1+x$ power $n$ ki asli value tabhi banti hai jab $x$ ka size one se kam ho. Us range ke bahar partial sums phat jaate hain aur expansion bemaani hai. Yeh convergence condition koi technicality nahi jise aap tal sako.

Isse number line pe picture karo. Minus one aur one ke beech, series converge karti hai — woh green band safe zone hai. One pe ya usse aage kisi bhi direction mein, yeh diverge karti hai. Toh series use karne se pehle, hamesha binomial ko aise arrange karo ki chhoti quantity $x$ slot mein baithe aur us band ke andar rahe.

Iss subtopic mein le jaane ke liye ek pakka rule: yahan koi $n\,C\,r$ symbols nahi, kyunki $n\,C\,r$ undefined hai jab $n$ negative ya fractional ho. Aap iske bajaye falling-factorial coefficient use karte ho. Jab bhi aap khud ko combination symbol likhte pakdo jiske upar non-integer ho, ruk jao — woh galat tool hai.
Yeh raha any-index ka formula sheet. Yahan sab kuch iss condition ke neeche hai ki $x$ ka size one se kam ho — isse har line pe ek permanent footnote ki tarah rakho.

General binomial series: $1+x$ power $n$ equals one, plus $n$ $x$, plus $n$ into $n-1$ upon two factorial, $x$ square, plus $n$ into $n-1$ into $n-2$ upon three factorial, $x$ cube, aur hamesha aage. Yeh pehle jaisa hi shape hai, bas falling-factorial coefficients ke saath jo kabhi terminate nahi hote.

General term wahi pattern follow karta hai: $T$ $r+1$ hai $n$ into $n-1$, neeche $n-r+1$ tak, upon $r$ factorial, into $x$ power $r$. Ab $r$ saare non-negative integers pe chalta hai, koi upper limit nahi.

Chaar special expansions seedha ratt karne layak hain. $1-x$ power minus one hai one plus $x$ plus $x$ square aise hi — geometric series. $1+x$ power minus one wahi hai alternating signs ke saath, one minus $x$ plus $x$ square minus.

$1-x$ power minus two hai one plus two $x$ plus three $x$ square, iska general term hai $r+1$ into $x$ power $r$. Aur $1+x$ power minus two wahi hai alternating signs ke saath. Yeh chaaron baar-baar aate hain, toh inhe pakka yaad rakho.

General negative integer power ke liye, $1-x$ power minus $p$ equals $p+r-1$ choose $r$, into $x$ power $r$, ka sum. Yeh saaf combination form negative-integer powers ke liye sahi tool hai — kahin koi undefined symbol nahi.

Aur poore applications side ka workhorse: jab $x$ ka size bahut chhota ho, linear term ke aage sab negligible hai, toh $1+x$ power $n$ lagbhag $1+nx$ hai. Wahi ek line har estimation problem chalati hai.

Cast: $n$ ab koi rational index hai, positive, negative, ya fractional; $r$ unbounded hai kyunki series infinite hai; aur hamesha ki tarah har quantity pure number hai. Convergence condition attached rakho aur yeh formulas use karne ko safe hain.

Pehla, series aakhir continue kyun hoti hai. Falling-factorial form mein likha general term kisi bhi real $n$ ke liye defined hai. Jo termination humne positive integers ke liye dekha woh bas special case hai jahan factor $n-n$ $r$ equals $n$ ke aage sab kuch maar deta hai. Us ittefaaq ko hatao aur series naturally hamesha chalti hai.

Slick step yeh hai ki teesri equation ko doosri ke square se divide karo. Saara scaling cancel ho jaata hai, ek side pe $n-1$ upon two-$n$ chhod ke. Us single ratio ko $n$ ke liye solve karo, phir $y$ nikaalo — aur series sum hoti hai one plus $y$, power $n$.

Chauthi, approximation. Chhote $x$ ke liye, linear term ke baad truncate karo: one plus $n$ $x$. Agar question zyada precision maange, agla term bhi rakho, $n$ into $n-1$ upon two, $x$ square. Jitne terms rakho woh maangi gayi accuracy se match karo.

$n$ equals minus two ko general series mein daalo. Terms hain one, plus minus two $x$, plus minus two into minus three upon two factorial, $x$ square, plus minus two into minus three into minus four upon three factorial, $x$ cube. Bas har falling-factorial product mein signs ke saath savdhaan raho.

Example two JEE Main favourite hai: $1-2x$, power minus three, mein $x$ power four ka coefficient nikaalo.

Toh $x$ power four ka coefficient hai fifteen into sixteen, jo two-hundred-forty. Combination ne fifteen diya; substituted variable ne sixteen diya; dono ko multiply karo.

Move yeh hai ki ek perfect fourth power ke bagal mein baitho. Two-fifty-five hai two-fifty-six minus one, jo two-fifty-six into one minus one upon two-fifty-six hai. Aur two-fifty-six hai four power four — ek saaf fourth power jise hum bahar nikaal sakte hain.

Ek jungli-dikhne wala sum ek saaf surd mein dhah jaata hai.

board_events.text: The four ways this subtopic bites
Ignoring $|x|<1$: the series is meaningless outside it — always make the smaller part the '$x$'.
Writing $\binom{n}{r}$ for non-integer $n$ — undefined. Use the falling factorial or $\binom{p+r-1}{r}$.
Forgetting to factor out the leading term of $(a+b)^n$ before applying the series.
Over-truncating: $1+nx$ is first-order only; keep $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}x^2$ when more precision is needed.
Pro-Tip: to sum a numeric series, use $\dfrac{\text{3rd}}{(\text{2nd})^2}=\dfrac{n-1}{2n}$ — one ratio gives $n$.
Memory aid: non-integer power $\to$ infinite series, only if $|x|<1$, and never write $\binom{n}{r}$.
Splitting a number into a clean piece plus a tiny piece
To find $7^{103}\bmod 25$: rewrite the base so it is almost a multiple of the divisor.
In $(K\pm1)^n$ all but the last term carry a factor of $K$ — mod $K$ they are invisible.

The conjugate is a tiny positive number (below 1), which pins down both the integer and fractional parts.

The identities that power every application
Modulo $K$ (or $K^2$), only the lowest-power terms in $K$ survive.
$n\in\mathbb{N}$; $K,a,b,p,q$ integers; $I$ integer part, $f$ fractional part — pure numbers.
Remainder · last digits · divisibility · parts
Remainder of $a^n\bmod m$: express $a$ (or a power of $a$) as $K\pm1$ with $K$ a multiple of $m$; expand; drop $K$-terms.
Last two digits $=$ value $\bmod 100$: choose $K$ a multiple of $100$; keep terms until one first becomes divisible by $100$.
Divisibility proof: expand as $(K\pm1)^n$ and show every surviving term carries the factor $m$.
Parts: set $I+f=(p+\sqrt q)^n$, $f'=(p-\sqrt q)^n$; verify $0<f'<1$; add/subtract to an integer; deduce $f'=1-f$.
Negative remainders: shift into $0$ to $m-1$ (e.g. $-7\equiv 18\pmod{25}$).
Golden move: make the divisor appear inside the bracket, then everything with it disappears.

Trap: computing powers of 7 directly. Spot $7^2=50-1$ so the modulus sits inside.

segments.text: Let's close any-index with the four ways it bites. These are conceptual, not arithmetic — which is exactly why they cost so many marks.

Trap one, ignoring the size of x being less than one. The any-index series is only valid inside that band; applying it outside gives pure nonsense. Always arrange the binomial so the smaller part plays the role of x and stays inside the region of convergence.

Trap two, writing n C r when n is non-integer. That symbol is undefined for a negative or fractional n — there's no such combination. Use the falling-factorial general term, or the p plus r minus one choose r form for a negative integer power.

Trap three, forgetting to factor out the leading term. For a plus b to the n you must first write it as a to the n, times one plus b over a, to the n. Applying the series directly to a plus b, without that leading one, is simply wrong.

Trap four, over-truncating the approximation. One plus n x is first-order only. If the question demands more precision, you must keep the next term, n times n minus one over two, x squared. Match how many terms you keep to the accuracy being asked.

And the pro-tip that makes series identification quick: divide the third term by the square of the second. That single ratio equals n minus one over two n, from which n falls out immediately, and then y follows. One division does the heavy lifting.

Hold one memory line and you'll stay safe: a non-integer power means an infinite series, valid only when the size of x is less than one, and you never write a combination symbol. Say it once and the whole subtopic stays honest.

<curious> Here's a question that seems to have nothing to do with expansions: what's the remainder when seven to the hundred and third is divided by twenty five? There's no x anywhere. Yet the binomial theorem cracks it, because it lets you split a number into a big clean piece plus a tiny piece.

The trick is always the same: rewrite the base so it's almost a multiple of the divisor. We want seven to the hundred three, modulo twenty five. Seven alone isn't near a multiple of twenty five — but a power of seven can be.

Watch. Seven squared is forty nine, which is fifty minus one, and fifty is a multiple of twenty five. So rewrite seven to the hundred three as seven times seven squared, to the fifty first, which is seven times fifty minus one, to the fifty first. Now the divisor is hiding inside the bracket.

And that's the whole engine. When you expand fifty minus one to the fifty first by the binomial theorem, every single term except the last carries a factor of fifty — and fifty is a multiple of twenty five. So modulo twenty five, all of those terms are simply invisible.

Picture the expansion as a sieve. Every term that carries the K — here fifty — gets struck out when you reduce mod K, because it's divisible by the modulus. Only the last term, the bare constant, survives the sieve. So divisibility, remainder, and last-digit questions all reduce to: which one or two terms are left standing?

The integral and fractional part problems use a sister idea. A number like seven plus four root three, to the n, is irrational. But if you add its conjugate, seven minus four root three, to the n, the irrational parts cancel exactly and you're left with a whole number.

And here's the clever part. That conjugate, seven minus four root three, is a tiny positive number, less than one. So when you know the sum is a whole number and one piece is a small fraction, you can pin down exactly what the integer part and the fractional part must be.

One safety check you must never skip: the conjugate trick only works if the conjugate genuinely lies strictly between zero and one. So before you use it, verify that p minus root q is between zero and one. Skip that and the whole argument can collapse.
Here are the identities that power every application in this subtopic. There are really two ideas: base-splitting for divisibility, and the conjugate identity for parts.

The base-splitting identity: K plus or minus one, to the n, equals the sum of n C r, times K to the r, times plus or minus one to the n minus r. You write the base as a multiple of the divisor, K, plus or minus one, and expand.
The point of that form: modulo K, or modulo K squared for last-two-digit work, only the lowest-power terms in K survive. Every term with a high power of K is divisible by the modulus and drops out.

A very useful special case: one plus K, to the n, is congruent to one plus n K, modulo K squared. Only the constant and the linear-in-K term survive when you reduce mod K squared. This handles a huge fraction of remainder problems in one line.

Two divisibility facts worth keeping: a to the n minus one is always divisible by a minus one; and more generally a to the n minus b to the n is divisible by a minus b. Both follow from expanding around the right base.

Aur key product: $I$ plus $f$, into $f$ prime, equals $p$ plus root $q$ power $n$, into $p$ minus root $q$ power $n$. Woh conjugates multiply hokar $p$ square minus $q$, poora power $n$, ban jaate hain. Wahi ek saaf product aapko in problems ko exactly evaluate karne deta hai.
Cast: $n$ ek positive integer hai; K, $a$, $b$, $p$, $q$ integers hain; $I$ integer part aur $f$ fractional part. Hamesha ki tarah, poore mein pure numbers — koi units track nahi.
Chalo chaar procedures rakhte hain, har question type ke liye ek. Sabki wahi base-splitting reedh hai, par K ka choice aur rukne ka point alag hai.

Procedure one, $a$ power $n$ modulo $m$ ka remainder. $a$, ya $a$ ki koi convenient power, ko K plus ya minus one express karo, jahan K $m$ ka multiple ho. Binomial theorem se expand karo, mod $m$ reduce karo, aur har woh term drop karo jisme K ho. Jo bache woh remainder hai — usse zero se $m-1$ range mein adjust karo.

Procedure two, last two digits. Last two digits ka matlab bas value modulo one-hundred. Toh K ko one-hundred ka multiple chuno, expand karo, aur terms sirf usi tak rakho jo pehli baar hundred se divisible ho jaaye. Uske aage sab mod one-hundred invisible hai.

Procedure three, divisibility proof. Dikhana ho ki $m$ kisi expression ko divide karta hai, toh relevant power ko K plus ya minus one power $n$ expand karo, aur dikhao ki cancellation ke baad har surviving term abhi bhi factor $m$ carry karta hai. Agar har survivor mein $m$ hai, toh poori cheez $m$ se divisible hai.

Procedure four, integral aur fractional parts. $I$ plus $f$ ko $p$ plus root $q$, power $n$ ke barabar rakho, aur $f$ prime ko $p$ minus root $q$, power $n$ define karo. Verify karo ki $f$ prime zero aur one ke beech hai. Phir dono ko add ya subtract karo taaki surds cancel hokar integer banein, aur nikaalo ki $f$ prime equals one minus $f$.

Aakhir mein, asal mein compute karne ke liye, product identity use karo: $I$ plus $f$, into $f$ prime, equals $p$ square minus $q$, power $n$. Yeh ek daraavni irrational expression ko ek ordinary integer power mein badal deta hai jise aap seedha evaluate kar sakte ho.

Ek arithmetic reminder jo logon ko baar-baar phasata hai: remainders non-negative hone chahiye. Minus seven modulo twenty-five minus seven nahi hai — woh eighteen hai. Report karne se pehle apne answer ko hamesha zero se $m-1$ range mein shift karo.

Aur chaaron ke peeche ka golden move: divisor ko bracket ke andar laao. Jaise hi modulus K ki tarah usme baith jaata hai, usse multiply hui har cheez gayab ho jaati hai, aur sirf ek chhota surviving piece answer tay karta hai.
Example one ek saaf divisibility proof hai: dikhao ki eight nine power $n$ minus one ko divide karta hai, har positive integer $n$ ke liye.

Nine ko one plus eight likho, toh nine power $n$ hai one plus eight, power $n$. Isse expand karo: one, plus $n\,C\,1$ into eight, plus $n\,C\,2$ into eight square, aise hi eight power $n$ tak. Divisor eight ab pehle ke baad har term mein baitha hai.

Ab one subtract karo. Nine power $n$ minus one hai $n\,C\,1$ into eight, plus $n\,C\,2$ into eight square, aise hi — aur har ek term mein eight ka factor hai. Eight ko aage nikaalo aur jo bache woh integer hai, toh eight nine power $n$ minus one ko divide karta hai. Proof done, koi induction nahi chahiye.
Example two woh remainder classic hai jisse humne subtopic khola tha: seven power one-hundred-three ko twenty-five se divide karne par remainder nikaalo.

Power ko rewrite karke modulus ko expose karo. Seven power one-hundred-three hai seven, into seven square, power fifty-one — aur seven square hai forty-nine, jo fifty minus one. Toh yeh seven into fifty minus one, power fifty-one, fifty twenty-five ka multiple ke saath.

Fifty minus one power fifty-one expand karo. Aakhri ke alawa har term fifty ka factor carry karta hai, isliye twenty-five ka factor, toh woh sab modulo twenty-five gayab ho jaate hain. Sirf aakhri term, minus one power fifty-one, survive karta hai — aur woh minus one hai.

Toh seven power one-hundred-three congruent hai seven into minus one ke, jo minus seven hai, modulo twenty-five. Sahi range mein shift karo: minus seven plus twenty-five hai eighteen. Remainder hai eighteen.

Trap yeh hai ki seedha seven ki powers ghisna shuru kar do — haath se namumkin. Fast move hai yeh spot karna ki seven square fifty minus one hai, toh modulus twenty-five bracket ke andar aa jaata hai aur expansion saara kaam karti hai.

segments.text: Example three is a last-two-digits problem: find the last two digits of three to the four hundred.

Last two digits means the value modulo one hundred, so we want a base near a multiple of one hundred. Group the exponent: three to the four hundred is three to the fourth, all to the hundredth, which is eighty one to the hundred, which is eighty plus one, to the hundred. Now eighty is close to the modulus.

Expand eighty plus one to the hundred. It's one, plus a hundred choose one times eighty, plus higher terms. But look at those terms modulo one hundred: a hundred times eighty is eight thousand, which is zero mod one hundred, and eighty squared is six thousand four hundred, also zero mod one hundred.

So every term with r at least one vanishes modulo one hundred, and only the leading one survives. Three to the four hundred is congruent to one, mod one hundred. So the last two digits are zero one. A four-hundred-digit-scale computation, settled in three lines.
Example four is the Advanced parts classic. If seven plus four root three, to the n, equals an integer part I plus a fractional part f, prove that I plus f, times one minus f, equals one.

Define the conjugate f prime as seven minus four root three, to the n. Now check its size: seven minus four root three is about seven minus six point nine two eight, roughly zero point zero seven two. So f prime lies strictly between zero and one, exactly as the trick requires.

Add the two conjugate expansions. Every term carrying an odd power of root three cancels between them, leaving a whole number. So I plus f, plus f prime, is an integer. Since f is between zero and one and f prime is between zero and one, their sum lies between zero and two and must equal the integer one — so f prime equals one minus f.

<excited> Now finish. I plus f, times one minus f, equals I plus f, times f prime, which is seven plus four root three to the n, times seven minus four root three to the n. That product is forty nine minus forty eight, all to the n, which is one to the n, equal to one. The irrational scaffolding collapses to a perfect one.
Let's finish with the traps for the applications subtopic. The method is powerful but unforgiving of a careless setup, so guard these four points.

Trap one, choosing the wrong split. Match the bracket to the modulus. For a mod twenty five question, use a multiple of twenty five like fifty. For last-two-digits, use a multiple of one hundred. A split that doesn't expose the modulus wastes the whole method — the terms won't vanish.

Trap two, stopping the reduction too early. Keep reducing until only modulus-free terms are left. If a term still has a lingering K in it, there's more cancellation available — you're not done, and a half-reduced answer is usually wrong.

Trap three, negative remainders. Minus seven modulo twenty five is eighteen, not minus seven. A remainder must live in the range zero up to m minus one, so always shift a negative result up by the modulus before reporting.

Trap four, skipping the conjugate check. The parts trick only works if the conjugate genuinely lies between zero and one. So verify that p minus root q is between zero and one first. If it isn't, the deduction f prime equals one minus f simply doesn't hold.

And a powerful pro-tip: find the smallest power of the base that is congruent to plus or minus one modulo the divisor. That power sets a short cycle, and then you just reduce the exponent modulo that cycle length. For instance two cubed is congruent to one mod seven, so powers of two repeat with period three.

Hold the one-line memory aid and the whole subtopic stays simple: make the divisor appear inside the bracket, and then everything multiplied by it disappears. Every remainder, last-digit, and divisibility problem is just a hunt for the few terms that survive.

<curious> We opened this whole chapter with a counting story: multiply a plus b by itself n times, and each bracket hands you either an a or a b. The multinomial theorem asks the exact same question, but now each bracket offers more than two choices.

So instead of two options per bracket, imagine a plus b plus c, to the n. Each of the n brackets donates an a, a b, or a c. Everything else about the reasoning stays identical — you're still just counting how the choices can be made.

A single term now looks like a to the n one, b to the n two, c to the n three, where n one brackets gave an a, n two gave a b, and n three gave a c. And of course those exponents add to n, because every bracket donated exactly once.

Picture the three brackets, each offering a, b, or c. You walk along and pick one letter from each. The pattern of picks — how many a's, how many b's, how many c's — is exactly what determines which term you land on.

So what's the coefficient? It counts how many ways the n brackets can be split into those groups: n one giving a, n two giving b, n three giving c. That count is the multinomial coefficient, n factorial over n one factorial, n two factorial, n three factorial — the same arrangements-with-repetition idea from Permutations and Combinations.

And here's the beautiful sanity check. With just two parts, that formula collapses to n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, which is exactly n C r. So the binomial theorem you've used all chapter is simply the k equals two case of this bigger theorem.

Counting how many distinct terms appear is also a Permutations and Combinations question in disguise. A term is fixed by its exponent list, n one through n k, adding to n, each at least zero. So you're counting the non-negative integer solutions of that equation.
And that's the classic stars-and-bars count: the number of distinct terms is n plus k minus one, choose k minus one. Distributing n identical units among k slots — the same tool you met in P and C.

One caution. The term count assumes the variables are genuinely independent, with no hidden relations. If there's a secret link — like the base being a perfect power — distinct terms collapse together, exactly as one plus two x plus x squared to the tenth became one plus x to the twentieth back in subtopic two.
Here's the formula sheet for the multinomial theorem. It's short — four results and two reminders — because it's really one idea generalised.

The theorem itself: x one plus x two, up to x k, all to the n, equals the sum over all valid exponent-lists of n factorial over the product of the n i factorials, times x one to the n one, up to x k to the n k. The sum runs over every list of non-negative exponents adding to n.

The multinomial coefficient is the piece out front: n factorial over n one factorial, n two factorial, and so on to n k factorial — valid whenever the exponents sum to n. That's the count of ways to split the n brackets into the k groups.
The number of distinct terms is n plus k minus one, choose k minus one. That's the stars-and-bars count, and it depends only on n and the number of parts k — not on the coefficients.

For the common case of a trinomial, k equals three, that becomes n plus two choose two, which simplifies to n plus one, times n plus two, over two. Worth memorising, since trinomial term-counts show up a lot.

To get the sum of all the coefficients, just set every variable equal to one. The left side becomes k to the n, so the coefficients sum to k to the n. Notice this is a different quantity from the number of terms — don't confuse them.
And the unifying reminder: setting k equals two recovers the ordinary binomial theorem exactly. Everything you learned in the first six subtopics is the two-part special case of what's on this board.
The cast: n is the index, k is the number of parts, and the n i are the individual exponents. As always through this chapter, every quantity here is a pure number.

segments.text: Example three ek last-two-digits problem hai: three power four-hundred ke last two digits nikaalo.

Last two digits ka matlab value modulo one-hundred, toh humein one-hundred ke multiple ke paas ek base chahiye. Exponent group karo: three power four-hundred hai three power four, poora power hundred, jo eighty-one power hundred, jo eighty plus one, power hundred. Ab eighty modulus ke kareeb hai.

Eighty plus one power hundred expand karo. Yeh hai one, plus hundred choose one into eighty, plus higher terms. Par un terms ko modulo one-hundred dekho: hundred into eighty hai eight-thousand, jo zero mod one-hundred, aur eighty square hai six-thousand-four-hundred, bhi zero mod one-hundred.

Toh $r$ at least one waala har term modulo one-hundred gayab ho jaata hai, aur sirf leading one survive karta hai. Three power four-hundred congruent hai one ke, mod one-hundred. Toh last two digits hain zero one. Ek four-hundred-digit-scale computation, teen lines mein settle.

Example four Advanced parts classic hai. Agar seven plus four root three, power $n$, equals ek integer part $I$ plus ek fractional part $f$, prove karo ki $I$ plus $f$, into one minus $f$, equals one.

Conjugate $f$ prime ko seven minus four root three, power $n$ define karo. Ab iska size check karo: seven minus four root three lagbhag seven minus six point nine-two-eight, matlab kareeb zero point zero-seven-two. Toh $f$ prime strictly zero aur one ke beech hai, theek jaise trick maangti hai.

Do conjugate expansions add karo. Root three ki odd power carry karne wala har term inke beech cancel ho jaata hai, ek whole number chhod ke. Toh $I$ plus $f$, plus $f$ prime, ek integer hai. Kyunki $f$ zero aur one ke beech hai aur $f$ prime zero aur one ke beech, unka sum zero aur two ke beech hai aur integer one ke barabar hona chahiye — toh $f$ prime equals one minus $f$.

<excited> Ab khatam karo. $I$ plus $f$, into one minus $f$, equals $I$ plus $f$, into $f$ prime, jo seven plus four root three power $n$, into seven minus four root three power $n$. Woh product hai forty-nine minus forty-eight, poora power $n$, jo one power $n$, equal to one. Irrational scaffolding ek perfect one mein dhah jaata hai.
Chalo applications subtopic ke traps ke saath khatam karte hain. Method powerful hai par laaparwaah setup ko maaf nahi karta, toh in chaar points ki raksha karo.

Trap one, galat split chunna. Bracket ko modulus se match karo. Mod twenty-five sawaal ke liye, twenty-five ka multiple jaise fifty use karo. Last-two-digits ke liye, one-hundred ka multiple. Jo split modulus ko expose nahi karta woh poora method barbaad karta hai — terms gayab nahi honge.

Trap two, reduction ko bahut jaldi rok dena. Reduce karte raho jab tak sirf modulus-free terms na bachein. Agar kisi term mein abhi bhi ek lingering K hai, toh aur cancellation available hai — aap done nahi ho, aur aadha-reduced answer aksar galat hota hai.

Trap three, negative remainders. Minus seven modulo twenty-five hai eighteen, minus seven nahi. Remainder ko zero se $m-1$ range mein rehna chahiye, toh report karne se pehle negative result ko hamesha modulus se upar shift karo.

Trap four, conjugate check chhodna. Parts trick sirf tab kaam karti hai jab conjugate sach mein zero aur one ke beech ho. Toh pehle verify karo ki $p$ minus root $q$ zero aur one ke beech hai. Agar nahi, toh deduction $f$ prime equals one minus $f$ bas nahi tikta.

Aur ek powerful pro-tip: base ki sabse chhoti power dhoondho jo divisor modulo plus ya minus one ke congruent ho. Woh power ek short cycle set karti hai, aur phir aap bas exponent ko us cycle length modulo reduce karte ho. Jaise two cube congruent hai one ke mod seven, toh two ki powers period three ke saath repeat karti hain.

One-line memory aid pakdo aur poora subtopic simple rehta hai: divisor ko bracket ke andar laao, aur phir usse multiply hui har cheez gayab ho jaati hai. Har remainder, last-digit, aur divisibility problem bas un kuch terms ki khoj hai jo survive karte hain.

<curious> Humne poora chapter ek counting story se khola tha: $a+b$ ko apne aap se $n$ baar multiply karo, aur har bracket ya toh $a$ deta hai ya $b$. Multinomial theorem bilkul wahi sawaal poochhta hai, par ab har bracket do se zyada choices deta hai.

Toh har bracket mein do options ke bajaye, socho $a+b+c$, power $n$. Har ek $n$ brackets ek $a$, ek $b$, ya ek $c$ deta hai. Reasoning ke baaki sab kuch bilkul same rehta hai — aap abhi bhi bas gin rahe ho ki choices kaise ki ja sakti hain.

Ek single term ab dikhta hai $a$ power $n$ one, $b$ power $n$ two, $c$ power $n$ three, jahan $n$ one brackets ne $a$ diya, $n$ two ne $b$, aur $n$ three ne $c$. Aur zaahir hai yeh exponents add hokar $n$ bante hain, kyunki har bracket ne theek ek baar diya.

Teen brackets picture karo, har ek $a$, $b$, ya $c$ offer karta hai. Aap chalte ho aur har ek se ek letter chunte ho. Picks ka pattern — kitne $a$, kitne $b$, kitne $c$ — theek yahi tay karta hai ki aap kaunse term pe pahunchte ho.

sections.title: Why the counts hold, and how to extract a coefficient & Pitfalls

board_events.text: Two proofs and two techniques
Coefficient proof: expanding means picking one $x_i$ from each of the $n$ factors.
Term-count proof: each term $\leftrightarrow$ a non-negative solution of $n_1+\cdots+n_k=n$.
Technique 1 — coeff of $x_1^{a}x_2^{b}\cdots$: check $a+b+\cdots=n$ (else 0), then $\tfrac{n!}{a!\,b!\cdots}$.
Technique 2 — coeff of $x^m$ in $(1+x+\cdots+x^t)^k$: use $\tfrac{1-x^{t+1}}{1-x}$ with $(1-x)^{-k}$.
“Number of terms” assumes independent variables; related variables collapse the count.
Example 1 [CBSE]: distinct terms in $(a+b+c)^{12}$
Example 2 [JEE Main]: coeff of $x^2y^3z^4$ in $(x+y+z)^9$
Check the exponents sum to the index: $2+3+4=9=n$. ✓
Trap: using a single $\binom{9}{2}$. Three variables need the full multinomial $\tfrac{n!}{a!b!c!}$.
Example 3 [JEE Main]: coeff of $x^4$ in $(1+x+x^2)^3$
Check: $(1+x+x^2)^3=1+3x+6x^2+7x^3+6x^4+3x^5+x^6$ — palindromic, coeff of $x^4=6$.
Example 4 [JEE Adv]: coeff of $x^7$ in $(1+x+x^2+\cdots)^3$
Also $=$ number of solutions of $n_1+n_2+n_3=7$ — multinomial and stars-and-bars agree.
The four ways multinomial questions go wrong
Using a binomial coefficient for 3+ variables: coeff of $x^ay^bz^c$ is $\tfrac{n!}{a!b!c!}$, not $\binom{n}{a}$.
Forgetting the sum-to-$n$ check: a coefficient is 0 unless the exponents add to exactly $n$.
Confusing 'number of terms' $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ with 'sum of coefficients' $k^n$.
Hidden relations merge terms — the term count assumes independent variables.
Pro-Tip: for $[x^m]$ in $(1+x+\cdots+x^t)^k$, use $\tfrac{1-x^{t+1}}{1-x}$ with $(1-x)^{-k}$.
Memory aid: spread $n$ choices over $k$ boxes — coefficient is $n!$ over the factorials of the box-sizes.

segments.text: Let's justify the two counts and then turn them into two working techniques.

First, why the coefficient is that factorial ratio. Expanding x one plus dot dot dot plus x k, to the n, means going through the n factors and picking one variable from each, then multiplying. A given term, x one to the n one up to x k to the n k, arises every time we pick x one from some n one of the factors, x two from n two of them, and so on.

So the coefficient counts the number of ways to assign the n factors into labelled groups of sizes n one through n k. That count is exactly n factorial over the product of the group-size factorials — the arrangements-of-a-multiset formula. Sum over all valid exponent-lists and you have the theorem.

Second, why the term count. Each distinct term corresponds to exactly one non-negative integer solution of n one plus dot dot dot plus n k equals n. So counting terms is counting solutions of that equation.

And that's stars and bars: distributing n identical units among k slots gives n plus k minus one, choose k minus one. Both proofs are pure Permutations and Combinations — the multinomial theorem is really a counting theorem wearing algebra's clothes.

Now technique one, the everyday task: find the coefficient of a specific monomial like x one to the a, x two to the b, and so on. First check that a plus b plus dot dot dot equals n — if it doesn't, the coefficient is simply zero. If it does, the coefficient is n factorial over a factorial, b factorial, and so on.

Technique two handles the trickier shape: the coefficient of x to the m in one plus x plus up to x to the t, all to the k. Rewrite the bracket as one minus x to the t plus one, over one minus x, and pair it with the any-index expansion of one minus x to the minus k from subtopic five. That converts a messy collection into two clean binomial-coefficient lookups.

And carry the caution: the phrase number of terms always assumes independent variables. If the variables are secretly related — a perfect power, a hidden identity — distinct terms merge and the real count drops below the formula. Always check the base isn't hiding structure.
Example one is a direct term-count: how many distinct terms are in a plus b plus c, to the twelfth?

Use the stars-and-bars formula with n equals twelve and k equals three. That's twelve plus three minus one, choose three minus one, which is fourteen choose two. Fourteen times thirteen over two is ninety one. So ninety one distinct terms, and we never had to expand anything.
Example two asks for a specific coefficient: the coefficient of x squared, y cubed, z to the fourth, in x plus y plus z, to the ninth.

Before anything, run the mandatory check: do the exponents add up to the index? Two plus three plus four is nine, which equals n. Good — the term genuinely exists, so its coefficient is non-zero. If they hadn't summed to nine, the coefficient would be zero and we'd stop.
Now apply the multinomial coefficient. It's nine factorial over two factorial, three factorial, four factorial — the factorials of the three exponents. Set it up exactly like that.

Compute. Nine factorial is three hundred sixty two thousand eight hundred eighty. The denominator is two times six times twenty four, which is two hundred eighty eight. Divide, and you get one thousand two hundred sixty.

The trap here is reaching for a single binomial coefficient like nine choose two. That's the two-variable tool, and it's simply wrong with three variables. When there are three or more parts, you must use the full multinomial coefficient, n factorial over the product of the exponent factorials.
Example three finds a coefficient by direct casework: the coefficient of x to the fourth in one plus x plus x squared, all cubed.

Think of it as choosing, from three factors, some ones, some x's, some x squareds. Let n one, n two, n three be how many give each; they must sum to three, and the total x-power n two plus twice n three must equal four. Solving that pair of conditions gives exactly two exponent-lists: zero, two, one, and one, zero, two.

Each list contributes its multinomial coefficient. The first, zero-two-one, gives three factorial over zero factorial, two factorial, one factorial, which is three. The second, one-zero-two, also gives three. Add them: three plus three is six. So the coefficient of x to the fourth is six.

You can sanity-check by actually expanding: one plus x plus x squared, cubed, is one, plus three x, plus six x squared, plus seven x cubed, plus six x to the fourth, plus three x to the fifth, plus x to the sixth. The coefficient of x to the fourth is indeed six — and notice the coefficients are palindromic, reading the same both ways.
Example four looks like a multinomial but has a slicker route. Find the coefficient of x to the seventh in one plus x plus x squared and so on, forever, all cubed.

Recognise the bracket. One plus x plus x squared, continuing forever, is the geometric series, which is one minus x, to the minus one. So the whole expression is one minus x, to the minus three — straight back to the any-index tools from subtopic five.

And we already know that expansion. The coefficient of x to the r in one minus x to the minus three is r plus two choose two. For r equals seven that's nine choose two, which is thirty six. One clean lookup, no casework at all.

<excited> And here's the lovely consistency: that thirty six is also the number of non-negative solutions of n one plus n two plus n three equals seven. The multinomial viewpoint and the stars-and-bars viewpoint give the same answer, because they're the same counting question seen from two directions.
Let's close the multinomial with its four characteristic traps. They're all about not slipping back into two-variable habits.

Trap one, the biggest: using a binomial coefficient when there are three or more variables. The coefficient of x to the a, y to the b, z to the c is n factorial over a factorial, b factorial, c factorial — not n choose a, and not any single combination. Three parts demand the full multinomial coefficient.

Trap two, forgetting the sum-to-n check. A monomial's coefficient is zero unless its exponents add up to exactly n. Always verify that first; if they don't sum to n, the term isn't in the expansion at all, and you can stop immediately.

Trap three, confusing two different questions. The number of terms is n plus k minus one choose k minus one. The sum of the coefficients is k to the n, found by setting every variable to one. These are different quantities — read carefully which one is being asked.

Trap four, hidden relations. The term count assumes the variables are independent. If the bracket is secretly a perfect power, or the variables are linked, distinct terms collapse together and the real count is smaller than the formula. Check the base before trusting the count.

And the pro-tip for the awkward case: to find the coefficient of x to the m in one plus x, up to x to the t, all to the k, convert the bracket to one minus x to the t plus one, over one minus x, and pair it with the any-index expansion of one minus x to the minus k. That turns a messy multinomial into two clean binomial-coefficient lookups.

Hold the one-line picture and the whole theorem stays intuitive: you're spreading n choices over k boxes, and the coefficient is n factorial over the factorials of the box-sizes. Everything else is just that idea, counted carefully.

Pehle, coefficient woh factorial ratio kyun hai. $x$ one plus dot dot dot plus $x$ k, power $n$, expand karne ka matlab hai $n$ factors mein se guzarna aur har ek se ek variable chunna, phir multiply karna. Ek given term, $x$ one power $n$ one se $x$ k power $n$ k tak, har baar banta hai jab hum $x$ one ko kisi $n$ one factors se chunte hain, $x$ two ko $n$ two se, aise hi.

Toh coefficient ginta hai ki $n$ factors ko labelled groups mein $n$ one se $n$ k sizes ke assign karne ke kitne tareeke hain. Woh count theek $n$ factorial upon group-size factorials ka product hai — arrangements-of-a-multiset formula. Saari valid exponent-lists pe sum karo aur theorem mil gaya.

Doosra, term count kyun. Har distinct term theek ek non-negative integer solution of $n$ one plus dot dot dot plus $n$ k equals $n$ se mel khata hai. Toh terms ginna us equation ke solutions ginna hai.

Aur yeh stars and bars hai: $n$ identical units ko $k$ slots mein baantna deta hai $n+k-1$, choose $k-1$. Dono proofs pure Permutations and Combinations hain — multinomial theorem asal mein ek counting theorem hai algebra ke kapde pehne hue.

Ab technique one, roz ka kaam: ek specific monomial jaise $x$ one power $a$, $x$ two power $b$, aise hi ka coefficient nikaalo. Pehle check karo ki $a$ plus $b$ plus dot dot dot equals $n$ — agar nahi, toh coefficient bas zero hai. Agar haan, toh coefficient hai $n$ factorial upon $a$ factorial, $b$ factorial, aise hi.

Technique two zyada tricky shape sambhalta hai: $1+x+\cdots+x^t$, poora power $k$ mein $x$ power $m$ ka coefficient. Bracket ko $1-x^{t+1}$ upon $1-x$ rewrite karo, aur isse subtopic five ke $1-x$ power minus $k$ ke any-index expansion se pair karo. Yeh ek messy collection ko do saaf binomial-coefficient lookups mein badal deta hai.

Aur caution le jao: phrase number of terms hamesha independent variables maanta hai. Agar variables chupke se related hain — ek perfect power, ek hidden identity — distinct terms merge ho jaate hain aur asli count formula se neeche gir jaata hai. Hamesha check karo ki base koi structure toh nahi chhupa raha.
Example one ek direct term-count hai: $a+b+c$, power twelve, mein kitne distinct terms hain?

Stars-and-bars formula use karo $n$ equals twelve aur $k$ equals three ke saath. Woh hai twelve plus three minus one, choose three minus one, jo fourteen choose two hai. Fourteen into thirteen upon two hai ninety-one. Toh ninety-one distinct terms, aur humein kuch bhi expand nahi karna pada.
Example two ek specific coefficient maangta hai: $x$ square, $y$ cube, $z$ power four ka coefficient, $x+y+z$, power nine, mein.

Kuch bhi karne se pehle, mandatory check chalao: kya exponents index tak add hote hain? Two plus three plus four hai nine, jo $n$ ke barabar hai. Sahi — term sach mein exist karta hai, toh iska coefficient non-zero hai. Agar woh nine tak add na hote, toh coefficient zero hota aur hum ruk jaate.
Ab multinomial coefficient lagao. Yeh hai nine factorial upon two factorial, three factorial, four factorial — teen exponents ke factorials. Bilkul aise set up karo.

Compute karo. Nine factorial hai three-lakh-sixty-two-thousand-eight-hundred-eighty. Denominator hai two into six into twenty-four, jo two-hundred-eighty-eight. Divide karo, aur milta hai one-thousand-two-hundred-sixty.

Yahan trap hai ek single binomial coefficient jaise nine choose two uthana. Woh two-variable tool hai, aur teen variables ke saath bas galat hai. Jab teen ya zyada parts hon, aapko poora multinomial coefficient use karna hoga, $n$ factorial upon exponent factorials ka product.
Example three ek coefficient direct casework se nikaalta hai: $1+x+x^2$, poora cube, mein $x$ power four ka coefficient.

Isse aise socho ki teen factors mein se, kuch ones, kuch $x$, kuch $x$ square chun rahe ho. $n$ one, $n$ two, $n$ three ho kitne har ek dete hain; woh add hokar three banne chahiye, aur total $x$-power $n$ two plus twice $n$ three four ke barabar hona chahiye. Us pair of conditions ko solve karne se theek do exponent-lists milti hain: zero, two, one, aur one, zero, two.

Har list apna multinomial coefficient contribute karti hai. Pehli, zero-two-one, deti hai three factorial upon zero factorial, two factorial, one factorial, jo three hai. Doosri, one-zero-two, bhi three deti hai. Inhe add karo: three plus three hai six. Toh $x$ power four ka coefficient hai six.

Aap sach mein expand karke sanity-check kar sakte ho: $1+x+x^2$, cube, hai one, plus three $x$, plus six $x$ square, plus seven $x$ cube, plus six $x$ power four, plus three $x$ power five, plus $x$ power six. $x$ power four ka coefficient sach mein six hai — aur gaur karo coefficients palindromic hain, dono taraf se same padhte hain.

board_events.text: The theorem and its core properties ($n\in\mathbb{N}$)
Number of terms $=n+1$, NOT $n$.
These are pure numbers — no units, no dimensions.
Everything you need to locate the biggest
Solve that inequality for $r$ to locate the numerically greatest term.
$k$ not an integer $\Rightarrow$ greatest is $T_{\lfloor k\rfloor+1}$. $k$ an integer $\Rightarrow T_k=T_{k+1}$ (tie).
$a,b$ are the two parts, $x$ the value, $n$ the index, $r$ the term index — all pure numbers.
Every essential formula, one screen ($C_r=\binom{n}{r}$)
Backbone: symmetry $\binom{n}{r}=\binom{n}{n-r}$ and Pascal $\binom{n}{r}+\binom{n}{r-1}=\binom{n+1}{r}$.
Grab-and-go: rules, tools, and memory aids
$n+1$ terms; powers sum to $n$; symmetry $\binom{n}{r}=\binom{n}{n-r}$.
Greatest coeff $=$ middle; greatest term $=$ where the ratio crosses 1; $k=\tfrac{(n+1)|x|}{1+|x|}$.
Remainders: make the divisor $K$ appear inside the bracket; parts: $(I+f)f'=(p^2-q)^n$.
Mantras: raise the whole bracket · solve for $r$ first · read the weights, pick the tool · divisor inside the bracket.

segments.text: Now let's pin down the exact formulas. Everything in this section is for n a positive integer, so the expansion is finite and clean. This is your toolkit — write it once, use it everywhere.

Here is the theorem itself. a plus b to the n equals the sum, as r runs from zero to n, of n C r times a to the n minus r times b to the r. It is just the counting story from before, written as one compact sum.
The form exams love most puts everything on a single variable x. One plus x to the n equals one, plus n C one x, plus n C two x squared, and so on up to x to the n.
The binomial coefficient itself is n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, valid for r between zero and n. This is the same object written n C r or the bracket notation.

This next one is the workhorse of the whole chapter: the general term. The r plus one-th term is n C r, a to the n minus r, b to the r. Memorise it — almost every question reduces to plugging into this.
Burn in the count: a to the n expansion has n plus one terms, not n. The powers run from zero all the way to n, and that's n plus one values.

Two instant results from setting values. Put a and b both equal to one and all the coefficients add to two to the n. Put a equals one, b equals minus one, and the alternating sum collapses to zero for n at least one.
Finally, a reminder that keeps you sane: every quantity here is a pure number. There are no units or dimensions to track — the only bookkeeping is the domain of n and the range of r.
Now the toolkit. There are really just three formulas here, one for each flavour of 'biggest', so let's lay them out and label exactly when each fires.

First, the greatest binomial coefficient, which is pure parity. If n is even, the single largest coefficient is n C n over two, and it's unique. If n is odd, there are two equal champions, n C n minus one over two and n C n plus one over two. No x involved — just look at n.
Second, the numerically greatest term, found by the ratio method. The magnitude of T r plus one over T r is n minus r plus one, over r, times the size of b over a. That's the consecutive-term ratio.

You set that ratio greater than or equal to one and solve for r. That inequality tells you exactly how far the terms keep growing before they start to shrink — and that boundary is your greatest term.

Third, a clean shortcut when the binomial is one plus x to the n. Compute k equals n plus one, times the size of x, divided by one plus the size of x. This one number collapses the whole inequality into a single division.

Read k like this. If k is not an integer, the greatest term is T at the floor of k, plus one. If k comes out an exact integer, then T k and T k plus one are equal and both are greatest — a tie. Watch for that integer case; it's a favourite exam trap.

There's a close cousin for the greatest coefficient of one plus lambda x to the n, where the coefficients themselves are n C r times lambda to the r. Apply the same ratio idea: c r plus one over c r is n minus r, over r plus one, times lambda, set greater than or equal to one.

And the usual reminder about the cast: a and b are the two parts of the binomial, x is the value you plug in, n is the index, r is the term index. Every one of these is a pure number — no units to chase.
Let's pull the whole chapter onto one screen. Here C r always means n C r, and I'll walk each block in the order we learned them.

The foundation from subtopics one and two: the theorem itself, a plus b to the n as the sum of n C r, a to the n minus r, b to the r; the general term T r plus one, your workhorse; and the term count, n plus one, never n.

The specific-term machinery. The net exponent E of r is p times n minus r, minus q r — set it to k or to zero. And the middle term sits at n over two plus one for even n, or splits into two terms for odd n.

The greatest quantities from subtopic three. The greatest coefficient is always the middle one. The numerically greatest term comes from the ratio n minus r plus one over r, times the size of b over a, at least one — and for one plus x to the n, the shortcut k equals n plus one times the size of x over one plus the size of x.
The coefficient sums from subtopic four, first batch. The coefficients add to two to the n; the alternating sum is zero; and the index-weighted sum, r times C r, is n times two to the n minus one.
The second batch of sums. The integration-weighted sum, C r over r plus one, is two to the n plus one minus one, over n plus one. And the sum of the squares of the coefficients is two n choose n.
The any-index results from subtopic five. One plus x to the n expands as an infinite series, valid only for the size of x less than one; and for small x, it's approximately one plus n x.

The applications from subtopic six. One plus K to the n is congruent to one plus n K modulo K squared — the remainder engine. And the conjugate product, I plus f times f prime, equals p squared minus q, to the n — the parts engine.

The multinomial from subtopic seven. The coefficient is n factorial over the product of exponent factorials; the number of terms is n plus k minus one choose k minus one; and the sum of all coefficients is k to the n.
And under all of it, the backbone: symmetry, n C r equals n C n minus r, and Pascal's rule, n C r plus n C r minus one equals n plus one C r. Master those two and the entire chapter hangs together.
Last stop — the grab-and-go cheat sheet. Everything you need in the last five minutes before an exam, with the mantras that keep you out of trouble.

Bedrock first: an expansion has n plus one terms, the powers in every term sum to n, and the coefficients are symmetric — n C r equals n C n minus r. If a row of coefficients doesn't read the same both ways, you've slipped.

The general term is T r plus one equals n C r, a to the n minus r, b to the r — and remember the m-th term uses r equals m minus one. That one off-by-one causes more lost marks than anything else in the chapter.

For any specific term, form the net exponent E of r, set it equal to k or to zero, and solve — but the answer only counts if r is an integer between zero and n. A non-integer r means the term genuinely doesn't exist.

The two greatests: the greatest coefficient is the middle one, and the greatest term is wherever the consecutive-term ratio crosses one. For one plus x to the n, jump straight to k equals n plus one times the size of x, over one plus the size of x.

The four headline sums: the coefficients add to two to the n; the r-weighted sum is n times two to the n minus one; the integration-weighted sum is two to the n plus one minus one over n plus one; and the sum of squares is two n choose n.

For any index, valid only when the size of x is under one: one plus x to the n is one plus n x plus higher terms, and for small x it's just about one plus n x. That approximation powers every estimate.

For applications, two one-liners: for remainders, make the divisor K appear inside the bracket so every term with it vanishes; for integral and fractional parts, use I plus f times f prime equals p squared minus q, to the n.
And the multinomial: the coefficient is n factorial over the product of exponent factorials, the number of terms is n plus k minus one choose k minus one, and the sum of coefficients is k to the n.

<excited> Finally, the four mantras that carry the whole chapter: raise the whole bracket, solve for r first, read the weights then pick the tool, and make the divisor appear inside the bracket. Keep those four in your head and Binomial Theorem is yours.

And the usual reminder about the cast: a and b are the two parts of the binomial, x is the value you plug in, n is the index, r is the term index. Every one of these is a pure number — no units to chase.
Let's pull the whole chapter onto one screen. Here C r always means n C r, and I'll walk each block in the order we learned them.

The foundation from subtopics one and two: the theorem itself, a plus b to the n as the sum of n C r, a to the n minus r, b to the r; the general term T r plus one, your workhorse; and the term count, n plus one, never n.

The specific-term machinery. The net exponent E of r is p times n minus r, minus q r — set it to k or to zero. And the middle term sits at n over two plus one for even n, or splits into two terms for odd n.

The greatest quantities from subtopic three. The greatest coefficient is always the middle one. The numerically greatest term comes from the ratio n minus r plus one over r, times the size of b over a, at least one — and for one plus x to the n, the shortcut k equals n plus one times the size of x over one plus the size of x.
The coefficient sums from subtopic four, first batch. The coefficients add to two to the n; the alternating sum is zero; and the index-weighted sum, r times C r, is n times two to the n minus one.
The second batch of sums. The integration-weighted sum, C r over r plus one, is two to the n plus one minus one, over n plus one. And the sum of the squares of the coefficients is two n choose n.
The any-index results from subtopic five. One plus x to the n expands as an infinite series, valid only for the size of x less than one; and for small x, it's approximately one plus n x.

The applications from subtopic six. One plus K to the n is congruent to one plus n K modulo K squared — the remainder engine. And the conjugate product, I plus f times f prime, equals p squared minus q, to the n — the parts engine.

The multinomial from subtopic seven. The coefficient is n factorial over the product of exponent factorials; the number of terms is n plus k minus one choose k minus one; and the sum of all coefficients is k to the n.
And under all of it, the backbone: symmetry, n C r equals n C n minus r, and Pascal's rule, n C r plus n C r minus one equals n plus one C r. Master those two and the entire chapter hangs together.
Last stop — the grab-and-go cheat sheet. Everything you need in the last five minutes before an exam, with the mantras that keep you out of trouble.

Bedrock first: an expansion has n plus one terms, the powers in every term sum to n, and the coefficients are symmetric — n C r equals n C n minus r. If a row of coefficients doesn't read the same both ways, you've slipped.

The general term is T r plus one equals n C r, a to the n minus r, b to the r — and remember the m-th term uses r equals m minus one. That one off-by-one causes more lost marks than anything else in the chapter.

For any specific term, form the net exponent E of r, set it equal to k or to zero, and solve — but the answer only counts if r is an integer between zero and n. A non-integer r means the term genuinely doesn't exist.

The two greatests: the greatest coefficient is the middle one, and the greatest term is wherever the consecutive-term ratio crosses one. For one plus x to the n, jump straight to k equals n plus one times the size of x, over one plus the size of x.

The four headline sums: the coefficients add to two to the n; the r-weighted sum is n times two to the n minus one; the integration-weighted sum is two to the n plus one minus one over n plus one; and the sum of squares is two n choose n.

For applications, two one-liners: for remainders, make the divisor K appear inside the bracket so every term with it vanishes; for integral and fractional parts, use I plus f times f prime equals p squared minus q, to the n.
